turns.reply: Welcome, glad you're here! When you snap a biscuit in half, what do you notice happen?

turns.student: it breaks into two pieces i guess
turns.reply: Two pieces, yes, that's the idea. Look at the diagram: a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei, giving out 2 or 3 neutrons. That splitting is called nuclear fission. How many smaller nuclei does the uranium-235 end up as?
turns.diagramCaption: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei. It gives out 2 or 3 neutrons.

turns.reply: Not quite — it splits into two smaller nuclei, like your biscuit snapping in half. The neutrons it gives out are extra bits flying off, not more nuclei. Say a large nucleus splits and the two halves are roughly equal in size. What would you expect those two smaller nuclei to be like compared with each other?

Sorry, that was a lot. The two smaller nuclei come out roughly equal in size, like two halves of a biscuit. The two nuclei and the neutrons are the fission products, the bits made when it splits. How many neutrons come out when a nucleus splits?

Yes — 2 or 3 neutrons is right. Uranium-235 is a fuel used in nuclear reactors, because it splits easily once it absorbs a neutron. So if a uranium-235 nucleus is just sitting there, what has to happen to it before it splits?

turns.student: it has to get hit by another nucleus?
turns.reply: This bit is a tricky one, so no worries. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?

Usually a nucleus has to absorb a neutron first, not be hit by another nucleus. Then it splits, giving out gamma rays and lots of energy, and all the fission products have kinetic energy. The fuels are uranium-235 and plutonium-239. Look at the diagram: each fission's neutrons can cause more fissions, which is a chain reaction. If each fission sets off 2 more, what happens to the number of fissions?
recap: Nuclear fission is when a large nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei.
It must absorb a neutron first, not get hit by a nucleus.
The two smaller nuclei come out roughly equal in size.
Each split also releases 2 or 3 neutrons, and uranium-235 is the reactor fuel.
turns.diagramCaption: Each fission releases neutrons that can cause more fissions.

turns.reply: Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it's moving. After a fission, the pieces fly apart at high speed, so they carry lots of it. Back to the chain: if one fission sets off 2 more fissions, and each of those sets off 2 more, what happens to the number of fissions?

Sorry, that was a lot. Now the opposite idea: in nuclear fusion, two light nuclei (ones with very few protons and neutrons) join into one heavier nucleus. Look at the diagram: two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, and energy is released. What happens to the two nuclei in fusion?
recap: Fission usually starts when a nucleus absorbs a neutron, then splits.
Splitting gives out gamma rays and energy, so the pieces carry kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy is the energy something has because it is moving.
Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are the fuels, and their neutrons can trigger more fissions.
turns.diagramCaption: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, and energy is released.

turns.student: they join together into one bigger nucleus
turns.reply: Yes — two light nuclei joining into one bigger nucleus is exactly fusion. So fission and fusion work in opposite directions: fission splits one large nucleus into two smaller ones, which matches your first guess. A memory trick: fusion sounds like "fuse", meaning join. If a nucleus splits into two smaller pieces, which of the two reactions is it?
recap: Fusion is when two light nuclei join together into one heavier nucleus.
Light nuclei have very few protons and neutrons.
Energy is released when the nuclei fuse.
Fusion is the opposite idea to splitting a nucleus apart.

turns.reply: Sorry, that was too long. Think of a biscuit: snapping it in two is fission, and pressing two crumbs together is fusion. If a nucleus snaps into two smaller pieces, which reaction is that?

Both reactions release a lot of energy, but they work in opposite directions. Fission splits one large nucleus into two smaller ones and powers nuclear power stations today. Fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier one and powers stars like the Sun, but isn't yet used for electricity on a large scale.

That's the end of this lesson. You answered questions on fusion and some on fission, and I told you the rest, including chain reactions and comparing the two. Come back any time.
recap: Fission is when one big nucleus splits into smaller ones.
Fusion is when two light nuclei join to make one bigger nucleus.
Memory trick: fusion sounds like "fuse", which means join.
Biscuit picture: snapping it in two is fission, pressing crumbs together is fusion.
